title: Toward Joint Optimization of Circuit Depth and Training Data Size in Adaptively Grown Quantum Classifiers
authors: Saeefa Rubaiyet Nowmi, Md Mahmuduzzaman Kamol, Mohammad Saidur Rahman
abstract: Building a quantum model involves a tradeoff: how complex the circuit should be, and how much training data it needs. Caro et al. show that models with fewer trainable gates need less training data to generalize well. Q-FLAIR shows that a quantum feature-map circuit can be grown gate-by-gate, stopping once further growth stops improving the training loss. We ask whether these two results combine into a predictable scaling law. Does Q-FLAIR's own stopping rule pick larger or smaller circuits as training data grows? Does the resulting generalization behavior track Caro et al.'s bound?   We reimplement Q-FLAIR's growth mechanism faithfully, including its analytic reconstruction and exact stopping rule. We run it on full-resolution (784-pixel) MNIST 3-vs-5 classification, at five training-set sizes from N = 2000 to 10000. We then fine-tune each resulting circuit, so we can measure Caro et al.'s notion of active gates, K.   We find no predictable relationship between training-set size and the circuit size Q-FLAIR converges to. Circuit size and test accuracy both vary non-monotonically with N, and seed-to-seed variance is nearly as large as any trend across N. The empirical generalization gap never exceeds Caro et al.'s bound in 14 of 15 runs, so the bound holds as a valid guarantee in those runs. But the gap correlates only weakly with the bound's value (r = 0.12). This shows that K does not explain most of the variation we observe. Why a valid guarantee can coexist with such weak predictive power remains an open question, and answering it may be necessary before circuit depth and training data size can be jointly optimized in practice.
summary: This work examines the relationship between circuit complexity and data requirements in quantum machine learning models using the Q-FLAIR growth technique. The authors found no clear, predictable scaling law connecting training data size to the optimal circuit depth. This suggests that jointly optimizing circuit depth and data size in practice is significantly more complex than current theoretical bounds suggest.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether a predictable joint scaling law exists between the required circuit depth and the necessary training data size for quantum classifiers.
main_result: No predictable relationship was found between the training set size and the circuit size converged to by the Q-FLAIR growth mechanism, suggesting that circuit depth and data size cannot be easily jointly optimized.
method: The authors reimplemented the Q-FLAIR gate-by-gate growth mechanism and tested it across multiple training set sizes on MNIST classification.
model_or_system: The model uses quantum feature maps within a Quantum Machine Learning (QML) framework, applied to a 3-vs-5 classification task on full-resolution MNIST images.
key_observables: Circuit size ($T^*$), test accuracy, and the generalization gap relative to Caro et al.'s theoretical bound.
important_parameters: Training set sizes ($N = 2000$ to $10000$), the number of active gates ($K$), and the dimensionality of the feature space (784 pixels).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the faithful reimplementation of the Q-FLAIR stopping rule and assumes the validity of Caro et al.'s generalization bound.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the non-monotonic variation of circuit size, test accuracy, and generalization gap with $N$, and compares the empirical gap against the theoretical bound.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of joint optimization, then details the faithful reimplementation of the Q-FLAIR growth process across varying data sizes, presenting results showing no clear scaling trend, and concluding with open questions regarding the interpretation of the weak correlation.
why_interesting: While focused on ML, the investigation into how complexity (circuit depth) scales with data size touches upon fundamental questions of model capacity and generalization, which are relevant when modeling complex quantum dynamics or emergent behavior in many-body systems.
